coefficients.label: Nile tilapia feed conversion ratio
sources: Shaw, Knopf & Kloas (2022), Sustainability 14(7):4064, DOI 10.3390/su14074064 (FCR 0.86–1.79 across protein sources)
Rodde et al. (2020), Aquaculture Reports 18:100349, DOI 10.1016/j.aqrep.2020.100349 (GIFT strain, individual rearing)
coefficients.note: Strongly diet-dependent; well-run commercial RAS ~1.4–1.8. Seed 1.7 is high-but-valid.

coefficients.label: African catfish (Clarias) feed conversion ratio
sources: African catfish (Clarias gariepinus) commercial/RAS/biofloc FCR ~0.8–1.0
coefficients.note: Air-breather, very feed-efficient. Seed 0.9 is mid-range. Split out from the old generic 'catfish' stub, which conflated this with channel catfish.

coefficients.label: Channel catfish feed conversion ratio
sources: Channel catfish (Ictalurus punctatus) pond/RAS FCR ~1.5–2.0
coefficients.note: US pond-aquaculture standard; less efficient than Clarias. Seed 1.7 is mid-range.

coefficients.label: Rainbow trout feed conversion ratio
sources: Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) literature FCR ~0.8–1.5 (trials report 0.99–1.49)
coefficients.note: Cold-water, efficient. Seed 1.2 is mid-range.

coefficients.label: Common carp feed conversion ratio
sources: Common carp (Cyprinus carpio) pond/RAS grow-out FCR ~1.5–2.5
coefficients.note: One of the most-farmed fish worldwide; seed 2.0 is mid-range.

coefficients.label: Barramundi (Asian seabass) feed conversion ratio
sources: FAO Lates calcarifer aquaculture species card: commercial FCR ~1.6–1.8, experimental pellet FCR 1.0–1.2
Barlow, C.G. et al. (1996) barramundi feeding/nutrition (lab FCR ~1.1–1.4)
coefficients.note: Fast, efficient warm-water grower; seed 1.6 is mid-band.

coefficients.label: Silver perch feed conversion ratio
sources: NSW DPI silver perch species note: FCR ~1.3–2.0, fingerling 1.2 to grow-out 1.5
Adebayo et al. (2005), Aquaculture Research 36:441–452 (cage feeding strategy)
coefficients.note: Australian aquaponics staple; seed 1.6 is near mid-band.

coefficients.label: Tambaqui (black pacu) feed conversion ratio
sources: Rodrigues, A.P.O. et al. (2024), 'Feeding rate and feeding frequency during the grow-out phase of tambaqui (Colossoma macropomum) in earthen ponds', Aquaculture Reports — pond grow-out FCR ~1.5–1.8
Tambaqui cage trials report FCR ~0.9–1.2 (cage vs pond natural-food intake)
coefficients.note: Amazonian flagship (FAO 589); seed 1.5 is mid-band.

coefficients.label: Giant freshwater prawn feed conversion ratio
sources: Macrobrachium rosenbergii grow-out FCR ~2.0–2.5 (decapods convert feed less efficiently than finfish; D'Abramo, Daniels et al. 2000, MSU Bull. B1030)
coefficients.note: The shrimp/prawn entry; seed 2.2 is mid-band.

coefficients.label: Striped/pangasius catfish feed conversion ratio
sources: MRC Mekong tech. symposium (2005): cage grow-out FCR averaged ~1.84 across three feeds (Pangasius hypophthalmus)
Water-temperature trial (2025), SVU Int. J. Vet. Sci.: juvenile FCR 1.22–1.28 at 24 °C up to 1.60–2.00 at 34 °C
coefficients.note: Among the most-farmed fish in SE Asia; seed 1.8 is high-but-valid.

coefficients.label: Lettuce feeding-rate ratio
sources: Rakocy/UVI raft guideline: 60–100 g/m²/day for leafy greens (lettuce originally 60 g, Bibb lettuce, 1988)
Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589
coefficients.note: Load-bearing sizing rule. Seed 60 sits at the conservative (low) end of the UVI band.

coefficients.label: Basil feeding-rate ratio
sources: Rakocy, Shultz, Bailey & Thoman (2004), 'Aquaponic production of tilapia and basil', Acta Hort. 648:63–69 (measured 81.4 g/m²/day batch, 99.6 staggered)
coefficients.note: Recalibrated from the earlier 70 g/m²/day stub to 85 — mid the UVI-measured basil band (81–100, Rakocy et al. 2004) — so a basil system is no longer under-fed.

coefficients.label: Tomato (fruiting) feeding-rate ratio
sources: Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589: fruiting raft ~100+ g/m²/day
coefficients.note: Fruiting crops carry a higher feed load than leafy. Seed 110 is mid-band.

coefficients.label: Kale feeding-rate ratio
sources: Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589; UVI leafy feeding-rate band ~40–100 g/m²/day
coefficients.note: Leafy band; seed 65 sits just below mid (range 45–90).

coefficients.label: Swiss chard feeding-rate ratio
sources: Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589; UVI leafy feeding-rate band ~40–100 g/m²/day
coefficients.note: Leafy band; seed 60 is near mid (range 40–85).

coefficients.label: Spinach feeding-rate ratio
sources: Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589; UVI leafy feeding-rate band ~40–100 g/m²/day
coefficients.note: Cool-season leafy; seed 55 is toward the low end (range 40–80).

coefficients.label: Cucumber feeding-rate ratio
sources: Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589: fruiting raft ~80–140 g/m²/day
coefficients.note: Fruiting band; seed 100 is near mid (range 80–130).

coefficients.label: Pepper feeding-rate ratio
sources: Somerville et al. (2014), FAO 589: fruiting raft ~80–140 g/m²/day
coefficients.note: Fruiting band; seed 100 is near mid (range 80–130).

coefficients.label: Lettuce edible yield (annualized)
sources: DWC aquaponic lettuce ~1.0–1.42 kg/m²/cycle (AUC thesis, fount.aucegypt.edu/etds/795); ~8–11 cycles/yr
coefficients.note: Per-cycle yields annualized — depends heavily on cycles/year (climate, cultivar). Seed 25 is optimistic-but-plausible for year-round warm-climate production.

coefficients.label: Nile tilapia harvest weight
sources: Common small-scale/aquaponic tilapia harvest target 0.4–0.6 kg (Somerville et al. 2014, FAO 589); commercial up to ~0.8 kg
IoTPond open dataset (data/empirical_envelope.json): observed max ~0.39 kg over a Jun–Oct grow-out at ~24.5 °C (below the 27–30 °C optimum)
coefficients.note: Seed 0.5 kg is a reasonable target, but the real ponds we ingested only reached ~0.39 kg — a sub-optimal-temperature grow-out finishes lighter than the target.
